retrieved_passages.source_excerpt: sec. 1: 'Exodus chapters 28 and 39 each offer expansive accounts of the priestly vestments and the process of producing them, with a set of four items prescribed for all priests and several others specifically for the High Priest.'; sec. 1: 'One possible function of the priestly clothing that generally does not have much purchase in the biblical account is that of atonement. This avoidance of expiatory language shifts when we look at the Amoraic period (late 3rd-6th century CE)'; sec. 4: 'This teaching runs through the four items of clothing worn by the standard priest and then the additional four garments worn by the High Priest, and suggests a sin ... for which each atones.'
retrieved_passages.retrieval_method: FetchURL public HTTP GET; article text extracted (abstract, sections 1-7, notes, references)
retrieved_passages.support_scope: passage-support: (i) the four-item priestly set plus high-priest additions is read as the biblical scheme by current scholarship; (ii) the garments' atoning role is not biblical but an Amoraic (late 3rd-6th c. CE) development, which is the layer-separation the entry's caution requires; (iii) the standard priest's set is priest-scoped, not a rule for Israelites at large
retrieved_passages.limits: Secondary scholarship; its own reconstructions (e.g. dating of the R. Simon tradition) are scholarly positions, not consensus recitations. It does not discuss archaeology or excavated garments, so it cannot speak to practice/compliance.

retrieved_passages.role: excavated dress (Iron Age, non-priestly): what dated textile evidence in the region actually looks like
retrieved_passages.source_kind: secondary-scholarly (peer-reviewed research article; Sukenik N, Iluz D, Amar Z, Varvak A, Shamir O, Ben-Yosef E, 'Early evidence of royal purple dyed textile from Timna Valley (Israel)', PLOS ONE 16(1): e0245897, published 28 January 2021; retrieved via the PMC mirror)
retrieved_passages.source_locator: Abstract; Introduction, subsection 'Early iron age textiles from Timna Valley' (opening paragraph)
retrieved_passages.source_excerpt: Abstract: 'The samples originated from excavations at the extensive Iron Age copper smelting site of "Slaves' Hill" (Site 34), which is tightly dated by radiocarbon to the late 11th-early 10th centuries BCE.'; Abstract: 'finds of dyed textiles are extremely rare, and those from Timna are the oldest currently known in the Southern Levant.'; Introduction: 'However, textiles are rare in the archaeological record. Like any perishable organic material, they are usually subject to rapid decomposition and their preservation requires special conditions ...'; Introduction: 'Starting in 2013, excavations in several copper production sites in the region by the Central Timna Valley Project uncovered dozens of fragments of dyed textiles, which currently constitute the largest Iron Age assemblage in the Southern Levant.'; Introduction: 'Their context - in a marginal region inhabited by semi-nomadic tribes, and within debris of copper smelting activities ...'
retrieved_passages.retrieval_method: FetchURL public HTTP GET of the PMC article page; abstract, introduction, methods and discussion extracted
retrieved_passages.support_scope: passage-support: the nearest dated textile evidence for the region is fragmentary (dozens of fragments), radiocarbon-anchored to the late 11th-early 10th centuries BCE, and from a non-Israelite, non-priestly industrial context (early Edom, copper smelting); it is fibre/dye evidence, not an ensemble that can be matched to Exodus 28's garment list
retrieved_passages.limits: Purple-dye chemistry and social inference are the article's subject, not priestly dress; the article nowhere claims an Israelite or priestly identification. Extraction was via the PMC mirror (publisher of record: PLOS ONE); DOI e0245897 read from the retrieval metadata/search record, not from a DOI line in the extracted text.

retrieved_passages.role: excavated dress (Middle Bronze Age dyed object): a dated textile object and its true evidential reach
retrieved_passages.source_kind: secondary-scholarly (peer-reviewed research article, Sukenik et al., 'Early evidence of an archaeological dyed textile using scale-insects: The Cave of Skulls, Israel', Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports, 2024, DOI 10.1016/j.jasrep.2024.104673 per the phys.org secondary record); ScienceDirect abstract page delivered Introduction and Conclusions sections
retrieved_passages.source_locator: Introduction (Cave of Skulls excavation paragraph; radiocarbon sentence; rarity sentence); 'Description of the textile' snippet; 'Conclusions'
retrieved_passages.source_excerpt: Introduction: 'textiles are rare in the archaeological record, like any perishable organic material, usually subject to rapid decomposition, and their preservation requires special conditions to prevent destruction by microorganisms.'; Introduction: 'In the Cave of Skulls, the fabric of the red-dyed textile discussed in this article (Fig. 2) was radiometrically dated to 3540 +/- 30 years BP, calibrated with INTCAL.13 ... to 1954-1767 BCE.'; 'Description of the textile': 'The red textile in question (IAA no. 2017-9071, L. 106, B. 1025) includes two small fragments (1.4 cm x 1.8 cm; 0.8 cm x 1 cm; Fig. 2) that belong to the same artifact.'; Conclusions: 'Despite the fact that these textile fragments measure no more than 1.5 cm, their significance is immense, as they bear witness to the utilization of scale insects for dyeing textiles during the Middle Bronze Age, the earliest of its kind known to date.'
retrieved_passages.retrieval_method: FetchURL public HTTP GET of the ScienceDirect abstract page (introduction and section snippets rendered); companion secondary retrievals: phys.org news report of the same paper (DOI 10.1016/j.jasrep.2024.104673; radiocarbon range 1954-1767 BC) and israelhayom.com report (18 July 2024) carrying the researchers' quotes
retrieved_passages.support_scope: passage-support: an excavated, radiocarbon-dated, dyed textile object exists in the region and is analysed down to the dye species (Kermes vermilio, kermesic acid), but it is a ~1.5 cm fragment from a Middle Bronze Age cave deposit - it establishes dye technology, elite consumption and trade, not an Israelite priestly garment
retrieved_passages.limits: The popular framing that ties this dye to 'the fabrics of the biblical Tabernacle and the priestly garments' (israelhayom.com/JNS wording) is press framing, not the paper's claim; the paper's own conclusion is about scale-insect dyeing technology and trade. The scarlets of Exodus 28:5 are a textual color term (tola'at shani); identification of an ancient red dye does not demonstrate that the prescription was executed. Extraction was of the abstract page (introduction/conclusions), not the full paywalled article body.
